title: An AI Tutor Study That Barely Tested Tutoring
author: Glenda Morgan and Phil Hill
summary: Glenda Morgan and Phil Hill critique a widely shared University of Maryland randomized trial that reported course-integrated AI tutoring lowered grades and LMS participation. They argue the title promises far more than the study delivers, and they unpack three claims: effects, tutoring and performance. Only about 15 percent of students offered the chatbot ever used it, so the average decline cannot be pinned on tool use. The tool defaulted to direct answers rather than guided tutoring, and the LMS integration was technical rather than pedagogical. Final scores and recorded participation are also indirect measures of learning. The authors conclude the real finding is that availability is not adoption and adoption is not evidence of better learning, and they warn that headlines are already misreading the result as proof that AI tutors harm students.
points: Only roughly 15 percent of students offered the chatbot used it, so lower averages across the whole treatment group cannot be attributed to AI use itself.
The tool was mostly an answer-giving assistant, with direct instruction as the default and only two instructors choosing tutoring mode, so the study says little about scaffolded AI tutoring.
Technical LMS integration is not pedagogical integration; the report itself admits instructors did little to build the tool into their teaching.
Lower final scores and fewer logged LMS activities are indirect measures that cannot show whether learning actually changed.
The usable lesson for ed-tech is that availability is not adoption, and how instructors integrate a tool matters more than the tool.
quotes: Sometimes a bad academic study is just a bad academic study, particularly when its title is misleading. We should be able to admit that.

The problem is that the report does not produce what it promises. It does not directly measure course-integrated AI tutoring, and while it may have included randomization, the treatment group did not take the same drug (i.e., AI tutoring).
That sounds consequential, but what, exactly, produced those effects? Only about 15% of students offered access ever used the tool—and only 13% in the same-course sample.
Among students who tried it, the average was approximately four sessions. About 40% had only one session, while a few heavy users pulled up the average.

Answering a course question is not, by itself, tutoring. Tutoring should attempt to find out what a learner understands, diagnose misunderstandings, and adapt explanations, hints, and practice accordingly.
And that “integration” really just meant technical LTI integration with the LMS, not integration into teaching methods. Yet “AI tutoring” gets top billing in the title.

EdTech isn't like some learning grenade you toss into ignorance and when it explodes people learn. EdTech was never a passive change-maker. EdTech is a tool, and how that tool is/isn't used is EVERYTHING.
That is a finding EdTech needs: availability is not adoption, and adoption is not evidence of better learning. What students do with a tool—and how instructors integrate it—requires attention.
